He had been proud and quick to speak, and he had wanted everyone in the building to see how clever he was. It had taken him several uncomfortable years, and a few bruising mistakes, to learn that a leader's cleverness is the least useful thing about him.

One winter the night crew completed the biggest order in the mill's history, and they did it a full day ahead of the deadline. A local newspaper sent a photographer to take a portrait of the famous head, but Mr Okafor politely sent him down to the packing floor to photograph the people who had actually done the work. The picture still hangs on the wall of photographs, and he is not in it.

Some years afterwards, a leaking roof let damp into a store, and an entire batch of paper was spoiled before anyone noticed. Mr Okafor gathered the workers together and told them plainly that the fault was his, because he had trimmed the repair budget to make the year's figures look better. There was no hint of excuse in his voice, and the silence in the room, he recalled, was one of the most respectful he had ever heard.

After that day, an odd and welcome thing happened: workers began to bring him their problems much earlier than before. They had learned that he would examine his own part first, and that no one would be shouted at for the crime of reporting something broken. Small difficulties were mended while they were still small, which saved the mill a great deal more than the repair budget he had once trimmed.

Tilda asked whether such humility was not simply a polite form of weakness, but Mr Okafor shook his head firmly. A humble leader, he said, may be fiercely ambitious for the company and entirely unconcerned about who receives the applause. The strongest people he had known were the ones who wanted the work to succeed more than they wanted to be admired.

Every Friday evening, Mr Okafor explained, he used to write two short lists on small squares of paper and carry them in his jacket pocket. One list named the people who had made the week go well, and the other named, without any decoration, the mistakes that had been his own. The habit was dull and a little embarrassing, he admitted, but it kept him honest through all of his years in charge.

That Friday Tilda tried the habit for herself, and the first name on her list was Joss, a packer who had quietly repaired a jammed cutter before the morning orders. When she thanked him, Joss looked so astonished that she wondered when anyone had last done it. By the end of the shift, three other workers had asked her shyly whether she knew who had really sorted out the delivery notes.

Mr Okafor described a visiting executive he had once met, a charming man who needed to be the centre of every room he entered. His staff fell silent whenever he spoke, and consequently he heard only compliments and never one useful warning. Tilda realised that a leader who fills all the space with himself leaves no room for anyone else's good ideas to enter.

Humility did not mean softness, Mr Okafor insisted, and he told her of a day when nearly everyone around him wanted to sign a grand-looking deal. The contract promised glory in the first year and a heavy burden for the following ten, so he refused it, in spite of the disappointed faces and the whispers that he lacked vision. Nobody ever thanked him for it, he said with a smile, which was precisely the point.

Marta told Tilda, as they shared a bench beside the loading doors, that Mr Okafor had never once raised his voice in all the years she had known him. Yet no one had ever doubted that he meant exactly what he said, and that was a rarer and more powerful thing than any amount of shouting. Tilda decided there and then that she would try to lead the finishing hall in that same quiet and determined fashion.

Mr Okafor told Tilda about a firm across the river whose leader had been famous, charming and very loud. Her portrait hung in every hall, her face was printed on every product, and every decision, however small, had to pass across her desk. For a time the firm seemed unstoppable, but it was a building with only one pillar, and everybody who worked in it knew that.

When that leader finally retired, no one in the company knew how to decide anything without her. Orders slipped, the best people resigned one by one, and the board argued for months about whose turn it was to be in charge. The firm did not collapse in a single dramatic afternoon, but it shrank steadily, year after year, until the portrait in the hall was the only large thing left.

Brightwell's founder, Eli Brightwell, was a quiet papermaker who disliked being the centre of anything. From the first year he wrote down, in a large grey book, how each task in the mill should be done, so that the whole place would never depend on him alone. His favourite saying, according to the old hands, was that a good mill should be able to run well on the day he stayed at home.

Tilda spent a lunch hour turning the pages of the old grey mill book, and she found that it was written in dozens of different inks and handwritings. Seventy years of workers had corrected it, argued with it and improved it, each one signing and dating the change in the margin. It was less a rulebook than a very long conversation, and she realised that the mill's memory lived in it rather than in any single head.

Every Monday morning, Tilda learned, one worker from each section of the mill sat down at a round table in the canteen to compare notes. The head of the company sat there too, but she was given no special chair and no special length of time to speak. Mr Okafor had begun the custom himself, because he believed that a good idea has no interest in who happens to be sitting at the top.

Mr Okafor remembered a time when he was ill and away from the mill for six whole weeks, and he confessed that he had returned half hoping to find it in some disorder. Instead he found the orders delivered, the machines running and the Monday table meeting as usual. His pride was stung for about a day, he admitted, and then he felt prouder than he had ever been, because the mill had not needed him to be brilliant.

Tilda wrote a single sentence in her notebook that evening and underlined it twice, which was that a good leader works to become less necessary. She looked at her own finishing hall and saw that nothing in it could run properly without her, which she had always taken as a compliment to herself. It now seemed to her a fault in the design, and one that she was determined to mend.

Tilda took a deep breath and asked Joss, the packer she had thanked a few weeks earlier, to lead the daily count of orders for one whole week. She sat at the back of the hall with her hands folded and tried with all her strength not to interfere, which turned out to be much harder than managing the count herself. Several times she opened her mouth to speak and then, with an effort, closed it again.

By Wednesday, Joss had quietly changed the way the count was done, and Tilda had to admit that his way was better than hers. He sorted the pallets by customer name instead of by date, and the hours of searching that used to swallow the afternoon simply disappeared. Tilda wrote the new method into the mill book, with Joss's name beside it, and felt her pride in the hall grow rather than shrink.

Standing at the gallery rail and looking down over the humming workshop, Mr Okafor summed up what they had learned so far. A strong company, he said, is built to outlast any single person, including the one at the top, and it does not need that person to be brilliant every day. What it does need is the right people around the table, and that, he told Tilda with a smile, was the subject of their next few Fridays.

On the next Friday Tilda asked Mr Okafor whether a company needed a brilliant plan more than it needed brilliant people. He answered, without a moment's hesitation, that people came first, though he admitted that most managers spend far more hours on their plans. He promised to prove it with a story from the mill, and then he reached for the teapot.

Years ago, Mr Okafor said, two crews were handed exactly the same new work schedule, which had been drawn up by clever people in the office. One crew read it, saw its flaws and quietly adjusted it to suit the machines, while the other followed it to the letter. By the end of the month the first crew had beaten its targets and the second had produced a mountain of waste.

No plan, Mr Okafor pointed out, can foresee everything that the world will do to a company, whether it is a broken bridge or a late lorry. One night the main supplier's delivery failed to arrive, and Marta's crew quickly borrowed pulp from a neighbouring mill and kept the machines turning until dawn. Nobody had written that solution into any schedule, because it had come from people who cared enough to think.

A good team, Mr Okafor said, can mend a poor plan as it goes along, learning and adjusting with every day that passes. A poor team, on the other hand, cannot rescue even the finest plan, because it will not notice when something is going wrong or care enough to put it right. That was why he had always spent his best hours on choosing people rather than on polishing documents.

When Brightwell hired someone, Mr Okafor explained, he looked first for two qualities, which he circled in her notebook: character and curiosity. Skills could be taught in a few months by a patient supervisor, whereas honesty and the hunger to learn were very hard to plant in a grown person. A candidate who had those two qualities, he said, could usually learn everything else that the job required of them.

To judge a candidate's character, Mr Okafor said, he always asked a simple question: tell me about a mistake you made, and what you did about it. The mistake itself mattered very little, but the honest or evasive way in which it was told could say a great deal. A person who claimed never to have made one, he added with a twinkle, was usually not worth hiring.

To spot curiosity, Mr Okafor said, he watched what happened at the end of an interview, when the candidate was invited to ask questions of their own. Someone who truly cared about the work would want to know how the paper was made, why the machines were arranged as they were, and what the night shift was like. The silent ones, he said with a smile, were usually thinking only of the door.

Tilda admitted that at her previous company she had once hired a dazzling speaker with the longest and most impressive list of qualifications she had ever seen. He turned out never to listen to anyone, and within a month the whole team was unhappy and two of its best members were looking for other jobs. She had mistaken a fine surface for a good foundation, she said, and she had never forgotten the lesson.

Mr Okafor said firmly that it is better to leave a chair empty for a while than to fill it with the wrong person in a hurry. The longest vacancy in the history of Brightwell had lasted eleven weeks, during which the rest of the crew had grumbled and covered the gap, but the person who finally took the job had stayed for twenty years. Patience at the beginning, he said, saves a great deal of pain at the end.

When one of the oldest packers retired at the end of the month, Tilda found herself with an empty place in the finishing hall and a notice to write. She composed the advertisement with unusual care, mentioning the work, the hours and the people, and she resolved to look for character and curiosity before anything written on a certificate. It was her first real chance to try what Mr Okafor had taught her.

Twenty applications arrived within a week, and most of them were polished, confident and full of the same fashionable phrases. One was plain and short, written by a young man called Sam, who explained that he had few qualifications but liked to make things and hated to waste them. Tilda read the letter twice, because it was the only one that sounded like a real person.

Sam arrived for his interview in a clean shirt that was a size too large and sat very straight in the chair, plainly terrified. He had fewer qualifications than any of the other candidates, but whenever he did not know something he said so, simply and without embarrassment. Marta glanced at Tilda across the table, and Tilda knew without being told that they were thinking the same thing.

Asked about a mistake, Sam described a day at a shop where he had dropped a full box of glasses on a stone floor. He had not hidden it, he said, because he could hardly have done so, but he had gone to the owner at once and offered to pay for the damage out of his wages. The owner had refused the money and given him a better job the following spring.

The following afternoon another candidate, whose qualifications were truly excellent, assured them with a charming smile that he had never made a serious mistake in his working life. Tilda, who had a particular fondness for honesty by now, found that this remark worried her far more than any story of failure could have done. A person who cannot see his own errors, she reflected, cannot be trusted to mend them.

Tilda and Marta discussed the two candidates over cups of tea, and they disagreed, politely, for nearly an hour. The qualified man would be useful on the first day, Tilda argued, but Marta replied that she could teach anyone to run a machine in six months and could not teach anyone in six years to be honest. In the end it was Marta's calm certainty, more than any argument, that tipped the balance.

Tilda offered the position to Sam, who accepted it with a look of such relief that she nearly laughed aloud. On his first night Marta stood beside him as he learned to feed a huge roll of paper into the great machine, speaking slowly and guiding his hands only when it was truly necessary. Sam listened to every word as though each one were precious, and he asked her, more than once, to explain why.

In his second week, Sam set the cutter to the wrong size and ruined most of a roll before he noticed his error. He walked straight over to Marta, told her exactly what had happened and showed her the damaged paper, long before it could be packed and sent to a customer. The loss was small, and Marta thanked him for it as sincerely as if he had done something clever.

Sam had the habit, which some of the older workers found tiresome, of asking why about everything he was taught. One evening his questions led him to an old step in the mill book, an extra wrapping of every roll in thick paper, which had been written for a machine the mill had sold years before. Nobody had needed that step for a very long time, and removing it saved the night shift nearly an hour.

Within a few months, Sam's plain honesty had begun to spread through the night shift in a way that nobody could have planned. Other workers started to admit their small mistakes much earlier, saying so before the error grew, and Marta noticed that the whole shift had become a little braver and a good deal calmer. Honesty, Tilda realised, is catching, and the first person to try it makes it easier for the second.

On Friday Tilda told Mr Okafor the whole story of Sam, from the plain letter to the old step that had been quietly retired from the mill book. He was delighted, and he said that skills grow with time and practice, but that character is the seed from which all the rest of a person's usefulness grows. Tilda added a line to her notebook, and, a little shyly, signed her name beneath it.

Tilda began to notice that Gil, a cutter who had worked in the finishing hall for more than twenty years, was missing his targets for the third month running. He had grown short-tempered with the younger workers and seemed to stare at his machine as though it had betrayed him. Everyone liked him, which made it very much harder for her to decide what to do.

Tilda described Gil's difficulties to Mr Okafor, half hoping that he would tell her to leave them alone. Instead he advised her to act soon, fairly and kindly, because keeping the wrong person in the wrong place hurts everybody, including the person himself. Waiting for a problem to disappear, he warned, is the most expensive plan that any manager can make.

Tilda invited Gil into the small office, closed the door and told him plainly what she had noticed, taking care to begin with what she respected in him. She did not scold or hint, and she did not pretend that nothing was wrong. When she had finished, she asked him a simple question that nobody had asked him for years: what did he actually want to do?

After a long silence Gil admitted that he was weary of the cutter and that what he would really love was to teach the young ones what he knew. Within a month he had moved to the training corner of the hall, where he explained his craft with endless patience and a growing sense of pride. A mismatch, Tilda learned, is sometimes the wrong seat and not the wrong person.

Mr Okafor then told her of a case where the right answer was harder, a manager who had bullied his team for months while Mr Okafor hesitated out of kindness. By the time he finally acted, three of the best workers in the mill had already quietly resigned, and he never fully forgave himself for the delay. The cost of waiting, he said quietly, is always paid by the good people who are left behind.

Good people stay, Mr Okafor said, when they are trusted with real responsibility and not just with orders. At Brightwell every worker had the right to pull a red cord and stop a machine whenever the quality of the paper seemed poor, and no one had ever been scolded for using it. The cord was pulled rarely, but its mere presence told every worker that his judgement mattered.

Fair pay was part of the answer as well, and every spring Brightwell compared its wages with those paid by other firms in the district. The results were shown openly to everyone in the mill, so that nobody was left to wonder or to suspect that a friend was being paid better. Mr Okafor said that secrecy about pay breeds suspicion, and suspicion is far more expensive than any wage.

Respect, Mr Okafor continued, also means telling people the truth in good time, before they have to hear it from a rumour. Whenever a change was coming, Mrs Hale pinned a plain notice to the board days in advance, explaining what would happen and why it was necessary. Rumours, he observed, are what grow in the silence that a leader leaves behind.

Marta herself, Tilda discovered, had begun her working life at nineteen, sweeping the floors of the mill with a broom that was taller than she was. Brightwell had paid for her evening courses and given her one new responsibility after another, until she had become the supervisor whom everyone on the night shift trusted. She did not tell the story as a boast but simply as an ordinary fact about the place.

Out of curiosity, Tilda counted how long the workers in the finishing hall had been at Brightwell, and she found that most of them had stayed for more than ten years. Mr Okafor was not surprised, and he observed that good people leave a bad place quietly and without a fuss, whereas they stay in a good place for decades. The length of time a company keeps its people, he said, is the best report on its health.

One evening Tilda stayed late to study the monthly sales figures for the whole mill, something she had never been asked to do but felt she should. One line on the chart sloped gently and steadily downward, and when she checked it she found that it was the envelope paper, which had fallen every month for eight months. Nobody had mentioned it to her in her first weeks at the mill, and she wondered, with a small chill, whether anyone had noticed it at all.

Tilda hesitated for most of the following morning before she could bring herself to mention the falling line. At her old firm, the person who carried bad news was too often the person who was blamed for it, and the habit of keeping quiet had followed her to Brightwell like a faint shadow. She told herself that this was a different sort of place, but she did not yet quite believe it.

On Friday she showed the graph to Mr Okafor, who studied it for a long time in complete silence and then thanked her sincerely for bringing it. He told her that her instinct to look at the figures was exactly right, and that her next step was to take the graph to the Monday table, where everyone could see it. Hiding a fall in the figures, he said, has never yet made the line climb back up again, and it usually makes the fall far worse.

On Monday Tilda laid the graph on the round table in the canteen, and a worker from the cutting section leaned forward and pointed at the falling line without the slightest sign of fear. Mrs Hale thanked Tilda for finding it, and not a single person suggested that the problem was anyone's fault. Tilda felt a weight she had carried for two days quietly slide from her shoulders.

Around the table, five people added their own observations, and each one made the picture a little clearer than before. Customers were buying cheaper envelope paper from huge factories, a driver reported, and Joss had heard several of them complain that Brightwell's thin sheets tended to curl at the edges. Nobody could have found all of this alone, but together they had assembled it in a quarter of an hour.

Mr Okafor explained that Brightwell kept a large sheet of paper on the canteen wall, known as the worry sheet, on which anybody could write a concern in any words they liked. No name was required, and Mrs Hale read every line of it each Monday morning before the meeting began. The rule of the house, he said, was that bad news should travel faster than good news, and the sheet helped it to do so.

Tilda remarked, rather thoughtfully, that facing hard facts requires a good deal of courage from everyone involved. Mr Okafor agreed, but he added that courage is far easier to find when people can see a path ahead, so every piece of bad news at Brightwell was accompanied by a plan for dealing with it. Honesty without hope tends to paralyse people, he said, whereas honesty with a clear plan has a way of energising them.

Tilda and Marta stayed behind after the meeting and drew a plan beneath the graph in thick black pen. They would visit customers to hear their complaints, test the curling sheets in the laboratory, and then decide together what ought to become of the envelope line. The falling line was still there above the plan, but it no longer looked like a verdict.

Tilda visited two of the envelope customers and listened carefully, resisting the urge to defend the mill. Both of them praised Brightwell's thick, heavy papers in warm terms, yet each admitted that the envelope sheets could not possibly compete with the great factories on price. It was a hard fact, and it was also a useful one, because it pointed towards something that Brightwell did very well indeed.

When Tilda reported what she had learned, Mr Okafor put down his cup and nodded slowly, with the expression of a man whose pupil has just passed a small test. The facts were now in, he said, and they were not pleasant, but they had cleared the ground for the real question: what should Brightwell choose to do, and just as important, what should it choose not to do? They would take up that very question over tea on the following Friday, he promised, and not a moment before.

Mr Okafor told Tilda that during his years in charge he had asked far more questions than he had given orders. One winter a certain machine kept stopping for no reason that anyone could see, and instead of shouting, he walked up to the crew and quietly asked them what they had noticed. The answers, he said, were in the minds of the people standing nearest to the problem.

His questions, Mr Okafor explained, were always the simplest ones he could think of: what do you see, what do you believe is causing it, and what do you need from me to put it right? None of them contained a hidden answer, a hidden complaint or even the faintest hint of blame, and that, he said, was the whole secret of their power. They treated the person who was asked as a colleague with knowledge, rather than as a tool that had stopped working.

Tilda tried the questions in the finishing hall, where one packing table seemed to jam every afternoon, and she asked the packer who used it what she could see. The packer pointed upward at a lamp that threw a shadow across the feeding slot just at the hour when the sun moved, so that nobody could see the paper begin to catch. A small lamp on a bracket, bought that very week, cured a problem that Tilda had been tempted to blame on the machine.

Mr Okafor offered Tilda a piece of advice that he said was harder than it sounded, which was to count slowly to ten in her head after asking a question. Most people, he said, rush to fill silence with their own opinions, whereas the person who waits is usually rewarded with the real answer. Tilda tried it that afternoon, and she was astonished at how much more people said once she stopped talking.

Every Tuesday morning during his years in charge, Mr Okafor said, he had walked through the whole mill from the loading yard to the boiler room, and he had made a point of knowing every person by name. It was not a duty so much as a way of listening without the formality of a meeting. Tilda decided to copy the habit in her own small way, and she chose Thursdays for her walk around the finishing hall.

Mr Okafor also made a habit of inviting those who had left Brightwell to lunch, a custom that surprised nearly everybody who received the invitation. He asked them, without defending himself or arguing, why they had decided to go, and he listened to every answer, including the uncomfortable ones. Several of the best changes in the mill's history, he told Tilda, had come out of those sandwiches.

Mr Okafor then set Tilda a new task, which was to find three practices in the finishing hall that persisted only because they had always been done. The question to put to each one, he told her, was whether Brightwell would choose to adopt it today if the mill were being founded that very morning. Most habits, he said, had once rested on a perfectly sound reason, and the only interesting matter was whether that reason still survived.

After a week of watching, Tilda found that every pallet leaving the hall was counted twice, once by a packer and once by a checker standing six paces away. When she asked why, Joss explained that the second count had been introduced years before, when a very old machine used to miscount, and nobody had ever thought to stop. They dropped it that week, and the hall regained a full hour of every working day.

Mr Okafor then gave Tilda a warning, which was that questions can be abused as easily as orders if a manager is not honest with herself. A question that already contains the answer the manager wants, he said, is only an order wearing a hat, and everybody in the room can see the hat perfectly well. A real question, he said, requires a real willingness to be surprised by the reply, and a real wish to learn something that one did not already know.

After a few weeks Tilda noticed that her team talked to her far more freely than it had done at the start, and with a good deal less caution. One of the older packers told her, almost shyly, that in thirty years of work at various firms nobody had ever asked him what he thought, and that he had a great many thoughts. She wrote on the board above her desk the words ask more, order less, and left them there for good.

Mr Okafor led Tilda to the old sample library and pointed to a tall shelf holding thirty different kinds of paper in neat rows. Long ago, he said, Brightwell had made every one of them, from thin wrapping sheets and glossy leaflets to heavy art card and cheap newspaper stock. He spoke about the shelf the way a man might speak about an old photograph of himself in a ridiculous hat.

The reason for the shelf, Mr Okafor admitted, was that every customer had asked for something slightly different, and Brightwell had said yes to every one of them. Saying yes had felt generous and exactly like growth, and at the time nobody in the company had questioned it. Each new order was a small victory, and the pile of small victories hid a larger defeat that was quietly taking shape.

The cost of all this generosity, Mr Okafor said, soon began to show in the mill itself. The machines had to be stopped and reset again and again for each new kind of paper, which wasted hours, wasted material and exhausted the crews, and deliveries began to arrive later than promised. Brightwell had become good enough at thirty things and excellent at none, which in business is a very dangerous position.

The turning point, Mr Okafor remembered, was a polite letter from a faithful customer, a bookbinder who had bought from Brightwell for thirty years. He wrote that the thick cream paper had once been the finest he had ever used, but that this year's deliveries had been uneven, and that he was sorry to say so. The letter was gentle, and it was the most painful thing that Mr Okafor had read in a long time.

Mr Okafor spent that whole winter studying the mill with a care he had never given it before. He asked three plain questions of every paper on the shelf: which of them did Brightwell make better than anybody else, which did customers value most, and which actually earned money after every cost was counted? The answers, laid side by side, pointed in a direction that he had half known for years.

One February morning, Mr Okafor picked up a thick pen and drew a bold line across the long list of products that was pinned to the board in the office. Everything above the line would continue, and everything below it would stop, a decision that felt dangerous and nearly impossible to defend to anyone who loved a sale. Only five papers remained above the line when he put the pen down, and the room was very quiet for a long time afterwards while the crew looked at the list.

For the first months, as Mr Okafor remembered it, the decision looked very much like a disaster. Sales fell sharply, two large customers took their business elsewhere, and Marta, who was then a young supervisor, remembered that the night shift had whispered anxiously in the canteen about whether the mill would survive. Mr Okafor never denied that he too had lain awake, and he said that anyone who claims to make such a decision without fear is probably not telling the truth.

By the second year, the turn had come, and it came slowly, in the way that all real improvements do. The machines ran for days at a time without being reset, waste fell by about a third, and the thick papers that remained became more consistent than Brightwell had ever managed. Customers noticed, and a few of the ones who had left came quietly back.

Today, Tilda observed, the same shelf held only five kinds of paper, set out with great care in neat rows and with plenty of empty space around them. There was thick cream book paper, heavy art paper, sketch paper, strong card and a folding stock for small books, and each of them was better than anything the mill had made in the old days. The empty space on the shelf, she thought as she looked at it, was not a gap at all but an important part of the design.

Saying no had cost something, Mr Okafor admitted, and he did not pretend that the cost was imaginary or the losses easy to bear. One customer whom he had politely refused had later become a close friend and a regular buyer of the mill's best paper, which he had never expected. Tilda wondered, as she walked home, why no always feels so much more dangerous than yes, when it is so often the more valuable word.

Mr Okafor explained to Tilda why he had kept exactly those five papers on the shelf and had let the other twenty-five go. Brightwell was better at thick, high-quality paper for books and art than any other mill within a hundred miles, and the rivals nearby had neither the patience nor the craft to match it. It was the one thing the mill could do that the world would miss if it stopped.

Part of the reason, Mr Okafor said, lay in the stream beside the mill, whose water was unusually soft and clean, as old Eli Brightwell had noticed when he chose the site. The rest lay in slow drying, patient testing and generations of careful hands, which no rival had ever troubled to copy. Good fortune had started it, he said, but only years of devotion had turned it into a real strength.

To keep the focus honest, Mr Okafor said, he had always gone out to meet the people who used the paper, and so he took Tilda to visit Mr Pell, the bookbinder who had once written the letter of complaint. The old man's workshop smelled of leather, glue and dust, and he greeted Mr Okafor as one greets a friend of forty years. Tilda felt, a little guiltily, that she was being let into a secret that very few managers ever learn.

Mr Pell explained, with a bookbinder's passion, why he had stayed loyal to Brightwell through all those years. The paper took ink without any bleeding, it folded sharply without cracking at the spine, and books made from it looked as fresh after fifty years on a shelf as they had on the day they were bound. He did not want the cheapest paper, he told Tilda; he wanted paper that would not embarrass him.

Next they visited an artist called Ines Varga, whose studio was full of half-finished paintings and jars of drying brushes. She told them that Brightwell's heavy art paper could hold a wet wash of colour without wrinkling or buckling, which was rarer than most people understood. She bought it by the box, she added, and recommended it to every student who walked through her door.

Walking back to the car, Tilda asked Mr Okafor what a rival could never copy, since any competitor could surely buy the same machines. He replied that machines are the easiest thing in the world to buy, but that years of patient craft, long trust and a name earned slowly cannot be bought at any price. Brightwell's real strength, he said, was made of things that rivals cannot simply order from a catalogue.

A focus, Mr Okafor cautioned, must also be able to pay its own way, and love of a craft is no substitute for sound accounts. Every month the mill examined each of its five papers in a plain ledger with two columns, one for what it earned and one for what it cost. A paper that was admired by everyone and lost money, he said, was a hobby and not a business.

One much-loved paper, the sketch paper, turned out to be losing money on every sheet, to everyone's dismay. After long discussions Brightwell began to sell it in larger packs at a fairer price, and it explained the reasons honestly to every customer on its list. A few customers drifted away, but the great majority stayed, and the sketch paper earned its place on the shelf.

Back in the finishing hall, Tilda decided to put the same question to her own team, and she wrote it in large letters on the wall: what are we best at? After many conversations at the packing tables, the answer that emerged was careful wrapping and stacking, so that no sheet left the mill with a bent corner or a smudge. It was not a glamorous skill, but it was the last thing the customer saw.

To protect that strength, Tilda made her first deliberate refusal, which was to stop relabelling goods for a small distributor, a side job that took up two afternoons every week. She explained her reasoning to Mrs Hale, who listened carefully, asked two sharp questions and then agreed with a smile. Within a month, the number of damaged corners had fallen noticeably, and Tilda understood at last why saying no can be a gift to the work.

Focus alone is not enough, Mr Okafor told Tilda on the next Friday, for it must be joined to discipline, which is the willingness to go on doing the same good things consistently for years. It is not an exciting quality, and it is rarely mentioned in newspapers, but it accumulates quality and trust until they harden into a reputation. Most companies, he suspected, fail not from a lack of ideas but from a lack of staying power.

At the beginning of every shift, Tilda discovered, each crew gathered around a short card of twelve plain checks, from the state of the blades to the cleanliness of the rollers. The card beside the great machine was stained with tea and thumbprints, and some of its words had almost worn away with decades of reading. Nobody found it interesting, and yet nobody ever skipped it, and that was exactly what impressed her.

At the end of the long production line, Marta stamped a small card for every batch before it could be loaded for delivery. No paper left the mill without a test, she told Tilda, and that rule, which was dull beyond words, had not been broken once in more than forty years. Tilda found it oddly moving to meet a promise that had been kept so quietly for so long.

Tilda watched as Marta cut a sample from a fresh roll and folded it backwards and forwards, again and again, until it finally broke along the crease. Then she weighed it, compared its colour with a faded standard card and laid a line of ink across it to see whether the edges stayed sharp. Each test took only minutes, but together they stood between the mill and any careless mistake.

Marta remembered one terrible day when a batch had failed its test just as a large order was due to leave, and the truck was already waiting at the gate with its engine running. Mrs Hale had held the truck, telephoned the customer herself, apologised plainly and promised a replacement within a week. The customer was not pleased, but he stayed, and he later told Mr Okafor that he trusted the mill more precisely because it had been willing to disappoint him.

Discipline, Mr Okafor stressed, must not be confused with rigidity, since the two are very different things. Brightwell was strict about the results that mattered, such as the tests and the checks, but its workers were quite free to find better methods of reaching them, as Joss and his pallets had shown. A disciplined company, he said, is one that is firm about its standards and generous about its means.

Mr Okafor described a firm he had once visited, where an entire shelf was filled with the folders of grand programmes that had been launched with enthusiasm and quietly dropped. Brightwell, by contrast, began very few new projects, but it finished every one of them, and each completed project became part of the mill's ordinary routine. Staying power, he said, is largely a matter of choosing less and then finishing everything that one has chosen.

Inspired by the card at the great machine, Tilda decided to begin each shift in her own hall with a five-minute meeting at which everyone could say what they needed. She kept it up faithfully for a month, on good days and bad ones, and slowly the workers began to rely on it, the way one relies on a clock. Consistency, she found, was not a dramatic gift at all, but a patient one that rewards those who keep their promises to themselves.

In the fifth week Tilda was busy with a large order, and she told herself that one small meeting could not matter, so she skipped it on Monday and again on Tuesday. By Friday the hall had become untidy, the packers were confused about priorities and two orders had been stacked in the wrong place. She restarted the meeting the following Monday, humbled, and learned how easily a good habit can be lost.

When Tilda confessed her lapse on Friday, Mr Okafor was not shocked, and he only smiled and said that every disciplined person has done the same at some point. Discipline, he said, is a gift to one's future self, and it may bore you to tears today but it will rescue you on the day when you are tired, frightened or tempted to hurry. That, he said, was why the card by the machine had never been allowed to fade completely.

On the kitchen shelf Mr Okafor kept a polished slice of an old oak trunk, and one Friday he took it down and laid it on the table between the teacups. Each ring marked a single year of growth, he pointed out, and not one of them showed any dramatic moment of transformation. Great results are built in that same way, slowly and almost invisibly, until one day somebody looks back and sees a tree.

Tilda noticed that the rings were not all the same, for some were wide and generous and others were thin as a thread. The wide ones, Mr Okafor said, were years of plentiful rain and the narrow ones were years of drought, yet the tree had kept growing through every one of them. A company, he said, should aim for exactly that, which is to keep adding a little in the lean years as well as the fat.

Mr Okafor remembered a year when impatient owners had demanded dramatic results from the mill, and he had been tempted to give them what they wanted. A loud new programme was launched with posters, badges and a slogan that nobody could remember afterwards, and it faded away within six months, leaving nothing behind except a cupboard full of unwanted badges. The quick fix, he said, with a rueful shake of his head, is always the most expensive kind of all.

To resist that temptation, he explained, Brightwell had adopted a simple rule of comparing each year not with the previous month but with the same year five years earlier. A single quarter, he said, tells you about as much about a company as a single ring tells you about a tree, which is almost nothing at all. Patience in judging, it seemed to Tilda, was the beginning of patience in acting.

To show how the opposite looked, Mr Okafor told Tilda the story of Redfern Papers, a rival across the county, and he reminded her that in this book, as in all the tales he told, the names were imagined. Redfern had been talented, well funded and admired, but it had chased every new fashion that came along, as though its only purpose was never to be left behind. The tale had no villain, he said, only a lot of clever people who could not stop moving.

Every year, Mr Okafor said, Redfern had changed its logo, its colours and its slogan, and each year it launched a new novelty, such as scented paper or glitter paper or a line that was supposed to be fashionable. Its customers soon lost track of what Redfern actually stood for, and its own workers, tired of one new programme after another, stopped believing in any of them. Nothing built merely to be fashionable, Tilda reflected, ever manages to stay fashionable for very long, because fashion moves faster than any company can follow.

In the end Redfern closed its gates, and Tilda and Marta drove past the empty yard one grey Saturday morning on their way to visit a supplier. A faded sign still hung over the entrance, and a pile of unsold goods, which had once been the latest thing, stood forgotten behind a rusted fence. Marta said nothing, and Tilda understood that she was thinking of her grandmother and of every worker who had lost a place.

Tilda asked whether all change was dangerous, since surely a company that never changed would stand still and slowly die. Mr Okafor replied that the difference was one of kind, because Redfern kept altering what it was, while Brightwell altered only how it did what it was. He promised to explain that distinction more fully, but first he wanted her to understand something important about time.

Small improvements, he told her, behave rather like savings in a bank, because a modest gain kept up year after year grows into something quite large. Over several decades Brightwell's waste had fallen by about half, not through any grand programme, but through the daily habit of fixing one small thing at a time. Hardly anyone had noticed it happening, he said with evident satisfaction, and that was the greatest charm of the whole method.

Tilda drew a chart of the damaged sheets in her hall and pinned it by the door, so that everyone could see the line wandering slowly downwards week by week. There were moments when she itched to announce a bold new campaign to speed it up, but she remembered the tree rings and the abandoned badges, and she held her tongue. Patience, she discovered, is not the absence of ambition but a particular kind of ambition.

One spring morning a salesman arrived at the gates with a gleaming new cutting machine strapped to a lorry, and he walked around it like a man showing off a prize horse. He promised, with great confidence, that it would double the speed of the finishing hall and halve its costs. Tilda, who ran the finishing hall, felt her heart quicken, and the workers standing nearby exchanged uneasy looks.

Tilda wanted the machine very badly, and she said so to Mrs Hale with more enthusiasm than she usually allowed herself. Mrs Hale smiled kindly and suggested that she should talk to Mr Okafor before she decided anything, and that she should bring all her excitement with her, since it would be useful. Tilda took the hint and arrived at the kitchen on Friday with a list of reasons.

Mr Okafor listened to her list with courteous attention, and then he observed that a machine is a tool and not a plan. Technology, he said, can only accelerate whatever a company is already doing, so that a company doing the right things will do them better, and one doing the wrong things will do them faster. Speed in the wrong direction, he added, is merely a quicker way to become lost.

Mr Okafor then gave her three plain tests to apply to any new machine that came through the gate. Would Brightwell want it if no rival had one, did it serve the mill's focus on thick paper, and would it make the people who used it better at their craft rather than merely replacing them? A machine that failed any of the three, he said, was probably a fashion in steel.

Mr Okafor told her how, years before, he had been offered an astonishingly fast machine for making thin paper, and how he had refused it, to the astonishment of his colleagues. It would certainly have earned money at first, but it would also have dragged the mill back towards the crowded middle of the market that Brightwell had worked so hard to leave. The machine itself, he said with a shrug, was excellent in every respect, and entirely wrong for the kind of mill that Brightwell wanted to be.

When Tilda applied the three tests honestly, the new cutter passed all of them, for it would help the mill to cut thick paper more cleanly and would need its workers' skill to run properly. Even so, Brightwell insisted on testing it on a small batch before it received a single full order, as it did with every new machine, however promising. Trust, as Mr Okafor often remarked, is something that a machine, like a person, has to earn by degrees and cannot simply be given.

The small test revealed a problem that nobody had foreseen, which was that the new machine nicked the corners of the very thickest sheets by a hair's breadth. The salesman, much less smiling now, took the machine's makers a message, and within two weeks a different blade arrived and was fitted at their expense. A full order sent through that machine on the first day, Tilda realised, would have damaged hundreds of sheets.

Some of the workers feared, quite reasonably, that the new machine might take their jobs, and the worry spread through the hall in whispers. Mrs Hale gathered everyone together and promised plainly that nobody would lose a place because of it, and she asked Joss and Sam to be the first to learn how to run it. Fear, Tilda noticed, shrinks wonderfully fast when it is answered with a clear promise.

Once the machine was running properly, it proved to be about a fifth faster than the old one, and the damaged corners almost disappeared. The hours that it saved were not used to push more paper out of the door but were spent on closer inspection and on training, a decision that Tilda made in the spirit of everything she had learned. The speed itself, she saw with some surprise, was the least valuable of all the things that the new machine had brought to the hall.

The old cutter was retired on a Friday afternoon with a small ceremony in the hall, and Marta painted its nickname along its side in careful white letters. Mr Okafor, who had come in specially, remarked that the question to ask about any machine was not whether it was new but whether it helped, and that Brightwell had been wise to ask it. Gil, who had worked beside the old machine for twenty years, wiped his eyes and pretended that it was dust.

One afternoon Mrs Hale took Tilda to a small locked room in the oldest part of the mill, where a sturdy strongbox sat on a shelf beside a thick ledger. This, she explained, was the mill's reserve, which was the money that Brightwell kept aside in good years so that it could survive bad ones. The room had no windows, and she said that this was by design, since a reserve was meant to be forgotten until the day it was needed.

Brightwell, Mrs Hale added, took a firm view of debt, and borrowed only for things that would repay themselves within a few years. Heavy borrowing made a company's good years look better than they were, she said, and its bad years far more dangerous, because the bank did not care about weather. The mill repaid its loans early whenever it could, even when the interest was low.

Mr Okafor's old rule, Tilda learned, was disarmingly simple: a good year is a time to fill the strongbox and not to empty it. Some part of every profitable season was set aside before anyone could be tempted to spend it, until the reserve was large enough to pay every wage in the mill for several months. It was a modest ambition, and it was surely among the most useful the company possessed.

Not everyone had admired the reserve, Mr Okafor confessed, and there were many quiet years in which it seemed to be a pointless hoard. A young manager had once begged him to spend it on a grand advertising campaign, arguing that money sitting in a box was money wasted, but Mr Okafor had refused and had explained why. The young man left a year later, and he was not entirely wrong, he conceded, only early.

In the second spring of Tilda's time at Brightwell, heavy rain began to fall on the valley and did not stop for eight days. The river beside the mill, which was usually so gentle that children paddled in it, began to climb its banks, and the workers glanced out of the windows with growing anxiety. On the eighth night Mrs Hale telephoned everyone on the list and told them to come to the mill.

That night the river finally broke its banks, and brown water crept across the yard and under the doors of the lower sheds. The workers formed a long line in the lamplight and carried rolls of paper, records and tools up the stairs to the higher floors, passing them from hand to hand without wasting a word. Tilda found herself beside Sam and Gil, laughing at a ridiculous joke and carrying a typewriter.

At dawn the floodwater stood knee-deep in the great machine hall, and the machines that Tilda had admired for so many months were half-hidden in brown water. Brightwell could not make a single sheet of paper, and everyone present knew that the mill would remain closed for many weeks. Nobody spoke for a long time, and then someone began quietly to ask what would happen about wages.

Mrs Hale climbed onto a crate in the yard, opened the ledger and told the workers, in a voice that carried perfectly well without shouting, that every wage would be paid in full. This would last for as long as the mill was shut, and the money would come from the strongbox that Mr Okafor had begun to fill years before. The relief on the faces around her was something that Tilda would never forget as long as she lived.

In the following weeks the whole town seemed to come to help, which was something that Mr Okafor said he had half expected. Neighbours, suppliers and even retired workers arrived with pumps, brushes, soup and spare hands, and together they scrubbed the mud from every floor and every machine. Brightwell had dealt fairly with these people for decades, and now, quite simply, they were returning the favour.

Two months to the day after the flood, the mill reopened, and the first roll of paper slid out of the machine to a roar of cheering that startled the pigeons on the roof. The strongbox was almost empty, but nobody had lost a wage and nobody had left, and Mr Okafor, standing at the back with his hands in his pockets, said quietly that it had done exactly what it was built for. The next task, he reminded them gently, was to begin filling it again, one good year at a time, starting that very week.

In April the old oak outside the kitchen window was covered in tender new leaves, and Mr Okafor used it to open the next Friday's lesson. The tree, he said, never changes its nature and changes its leaves every year, which was exactly how lasting companies behave. They hold on to a small core of values with great stubbornness and are willing to change almost everything else.

Three small signs hung on the wall of the oldest shed, painted by Eli Brightwell himself so many years ago that the colours had mellowed into a soft brown. They read honest weight, on time and fair play, and in all those decades nobody had ever suggested taking them down or adding a fourth. Those words, Mr Okafor said, were Brightwell's roots, and everything else was only branches.

Honest weight, Mr Okafor explained, meant that every ream held precisely the number of sheets promised on its label, and every sheet weighed exactly what the customer had been told. Years ago a single short ream had been discovered by an angry buyer, and old Eli had ordered the entire batch to be collected back and counted again, at heavy cost. He regarded it, said Mr Okafor, as the cheapest advertisement the mill had ever bought.

At Mr Okafor's request Tilda made a list in her notebook of everything that had changed at Brightwell since its beginning, and she was startled by its length. The machines, the roofs, the methods, the vehicles, the customers and even the way in which orders arrived had all been replaced at least once in seventy years. Only those three painted signs and the spirit behind them remained exactly as they had been.

A value, Mr Okafor warned, is not a slogan to be admired on a wall, because a value that never costs anything is only a decoration. Brightwell had once lost a very large order from a hungry buyer who wanted a cheaper ream with fewer sheets inside, and Eli's grandson, who ran the mill then, had refused without a flicker of doubt. The loss stung for a year, but the refusal was remembered by every other customer for ten.

Because the values were so few and so plain, Brightwell could hire people who truly shared them, and there was no need to force anyone to obey a long list of rules. Those who did not care about honest weight, punctuality or fairness usually left the mill of their own accord within a year or two, and nobody felt any bitterness about it. It was, Tilda thought, rather like a fence that nobody had to build, because the right people simply stayed within it.

A few weeks later Tilda stood before a small group of managers with a sample of thick, softly speckled paper made partly from recycled fibre, and she explained her idea for a new recycled line. It would be a change of method and not of purpose, she argued, since the paper would be heavy, cream-coloured and honest, in perfect keeping with the three signs. She had rehearsed the speech for a week, and her hands were nevertheless shaking.

An older manager called Rafe objected, quite fairly, that recycled paper was not what Brightwell did, and that the mill had worked far too hard to narrow its focus to be tempted by something fashionable. Tilda replied that the paper was thick, was meant for books and art, and was being requested by a loyal customer, and she laid Ines Varga's letter on the table. Rafe read the letter twice, set it down gently on the table and admitted, with a rueful half-smile, that this changed things considerably.

That Friday Mr Okafor checked the idea against everything they had discussed in the past two years, and he found that it held up remarkably well. It served the focus on thick paper, it fitted the three painted values, provided that every label told the exact truth about the proportion of recycled fibre, and it would make the mill's people better at their craft. He was, he said, truly delighted by the proposal, although he reserved the right to be extremely careful about how it was carried out.

Mr Okafor liked the idea, but he suggested that she should not bet the entire mill on it. Instead, they agreed to produce a modest batch for one trusted customer, and to watch carefully how the paper was received. If the test succeeded they would expand, and if it failed they would have lost very little.

Ines Varga tried the recycled paper with her students that autumn, and she wrote to the mill in great excitement afterwards, saying that the paint behaved beautifully and the texture was a joy. Brightwell made more of it, but slowly, giving the new line only one machine day a week at first, and watching every result with care. Within a year the day had become two, and nobody had been forced to take a risk.

In the mill archive Mr Okafor lifted down bundles of old delivery notes, tied with faded string and stamped, one after another, with the words on time. A reputation, he said, is not made by a grand announcement or a clever advertisement but by thousands of small promises that were kept without any fuss. Each of those slips was one tiny stone, and together they made up the foundation on which the mill stood.

Mr Okafor then told her about the night when a roll of the wrong shade of cream had gone out by mistake, and the customer had not yet noticed. Marta, hearing of it only at midnight, had loaded a replacement into a small van and driven three hours through the rain to deliver it and to apologise in person. The customer later said that he had never before been apologised to by someone who had so clearly meant it.

Kept promises, Mr Okafor said, make large promises believable, and he told her of the stranger who had once walked in and placed an enormous order without even asking for a discount. A friend of his had told him, he explained, that Brightwell was a company that did exactly what it said it would do. No advertisement in the world, said Mr Okafor, can buy a sentence like that.

In the yard one morning a lorry unloaded sacks of cotton and wood pulp, and Marta stood laughing with the supplier's driver as if they were cousins. Brightwell paid its suppliers on time even in the leanest months, Mr Okafor said, and treated them as partners rather than as people to be squeezed. Long relationships, he explained, are an advantage that no rival can copy in a single season.

Mr Okafor remembered a dry year when a shortage of pulp left half the mills in the region with empty storerooms and idle machines. Brightwell's suppliers delivered to it first, quietly, without being asked, because the mill had always paid them fairly and promptly. That kindness had cost Brightwell nothing in the good years, he observed, and in the lean one it was worth more than a year of profit.

The town, Tilda learned, was never treated as a mere backdrop to the work, for Brightwell bought from local shops whenever it could and welcomed school visits every spring. It also took on apprentices from the town each year, and a good half of the older workers had begun that way. After the flood, Tilda realised, the town's help had not been a surprise but the interest on a very old investment.

One Friday Tilda stayed late and joined the night shift for its midnight tea around a long table in the corner of the machine hall. Marta poured, someone passed round a tin of biscuits, and everyone in the room knew everyone else's name, as well as the name of the other person's dog. A culture, she thought, was not written in a handbook but poured into cups, one night after another.

At the end of that third year, which was a good one, every worker at Brightwell received a plain envelope containing a share of the profit, from the newest packer to Mrs Hale herself. The gap between the highest pay and the lowest was kept deliberately narrow, which Mr Okafor said was fair and also practical, because people who feel like partners behave like partners. Nobody boasted about the envelopes afterwards, and in a mill where everyone shared the result, nobody needed to do so.

Culture, said Mr Okafor, is simply what people do when nobody is watching, and he asked Tilda to see whether she could catch it in the act. That same evening she saw a young packer, alone in the empty hall and believing himself unobserved, stop to pick up a loose screw and tighten a wobbling shelf. He had not been asked, and he never mentioned it to anyone, which was exactly what Mr Okafor had meant.

One Friday afternoon, after a long silence, Mr Okafor announced that he would now tell Tilda about the biggest mistake of his life. He spoke quietly and looked out of the window at the yard as he began, as though the story were written on the bricks. Tilda put down her pen, because she sensed that this was not an occasion for notes.

Many years earlier, Mr Okafor said, the mill had been thriving, and orders had been pouring in faster than it could fill them. He was in his fifties by then, and the old pride that he thought he had mastered had crept quietly back in, bringing with it the dangerous idea that he could not be wrong. Success, he said, is the most persuasive teacher of bad lessons, and it teaches them in a voice that sounds just like praise.

He decided to build a second mill in the next valley and so to double the company's output at a single stroke, which seemed to him a brilliant stroke of ambition. The building work ran well over its time and well over its budget, and Brightwell, against its own rule, borrowed heavily to keep it going. Rain fell on the half-built walls through that whole autumn, and the cranes stood idle.

An old foreman named Bram came to him more than once and warned him, with great politeness, that the mill was stretching itself too thin and that the first mill was already beginning to suffer. Mr Okafor, who had asked so many questions in earlier years, did not ask a single one now, and he told Bram, rather curtly, that he worried too much. It was the only time in the whole of his long career that he stopped listening, and it was therefore the time that mattered most.

The orders, as it turned out, did not double at all, and the quality of the paper began to slip in both mills as the best people were stretched between them. Then, when the interest bills grew heavy, the bank grew nervous and asked for its money back far sooner than anyone had expected. Mr Okafor said that he had never felt so small as he did sitting in that bank, being politely told the truth.

Mr Okafor gathered every worker in the canteen and told them the whole truth, without softening a single word of it. The second mill had been his mistake, he said, his alone, and the company was in real danger of failing because of it. There was a long silence, and then Bram, the old foreman, stood up and said that he had a few ideas.

Together they agreed to close the half-built second mill, sell the land and the equipment that could be sold, and tidy up the rest as carefully as if they were putting away a child's toys. It was painful to dismantle what had cost so much hope, but it was, as Bram put it, the only honest way out of the trouble. Mr Okafor noted that nobody in the room had called him a fool, which made it worse.

Not a single worker lost a job in that crisis, because the managers took pay cuts first, and Mr Okafor himself drew no salary at all for two full years. He said that this was only fair, since the mistake was his, and that it was the most useful two years of education he had ever received. The workers, in return, gave the mill a loyalty that no wage could have purchased.

It took four patient years to repay every debt and to recover the mill's strength, and during that time Brightwell grew by hardly anything at all. From that day onwards, the rule against heavy borrowing was strict and never broken, and the practice of saving a part of every good year became the foundation of the strongbox. Tilda realised that the mill's famous caution had been bought with a hard coin.

Mr Okafor ended his story by saying that mistakes honestly faced can become the foundation of a company's wisdom, whereas mistakes hidden are simply repeated. Beside the old mill book, he told Tilda, stood a second grey book in which every serious mistake of the company was written down plainly, and his own second mill was the first entry. That evening Tilda wrote her own small entry about the skipped meeting, and she felt a little braver for doing it.

On a damp Friday in the fourth autumn, Mr Okafor took from his pocket a ring of old iron keys and told Tilda that he had handed them to Mrs Hale on the day he retired. Strong companies, he said, plan for their next leaders long before they are needed, and never leave such an important matter to luck or to the last minute. Brightwell had always grown its leaders from within, he added, as a gardener grows an oak from an acorn.

Eight years before he retired, Mr Okafor said, he had begun to look quietly for the person who would lead Brightwell after him. He had written down three names, and then he had given each of those people real responsibility and watched, without comment, how they handled it when things went wrong. The best test of a future leader, he told Tilda, is not an interview but a difficult year.

Two of the three candidates could hardly have been more different, Mr Okafor said, and everyone in the mill knew it. Corin Blake was brilliant, charming and quick, the sort of person who lights up a room, while Hale was quiet, steady and watchful, speaking only when she had something useful to say. Everyone expected him to choose Blake, and Blake expected it most of all, as it later turned out.

In the end he chose Mrs Hale, and his reasons, he said, were all to be found in the bad year of the second mill. While others had been tempted to soften the truth, she had kept the figures honest, asked questions of everyone, taken the blame when it was hers and shared the credit whenever it was earned. Those qualities, which are not the ones that a crowd applauds, are the ones that a mill can safely lean on.

Corin Blake was bitterly disappointed, and within a year he had left Brightwell to lead another firm, where, in the end, he did very well indeed. Mr Okafor said that this was exactly as it should be, because the choice had never been about who was worth more but about who fitted this particular mill at this particular time. He still received a card from Blake every year, and he was glad of it.

In Mrs Hale's office, on the wall behind her desk, hung four simple gauges with their numbers written in plain letters, and she explained that those four were the only figures Brightwell watched every week. They were on-time deliveries, faults in each batch, the number of staff who stayed, and the money in the reserve, and everything else was kept in the ledgers for those who needed it. Too many numbers, she said with a smile, mean that you eventually notice none of them, and a company that watches everything sees nothing at all.

Success, Mrs Hale warned, has a way of making a company comfortable, and a comfortable company stops looking out of the window for storms. That was why, twice a year, Brightwell stopped its work for an afternoon and asked itself what might hurt it in the next five years. The question was uncomfortable on purpose, she said, and its discomfort was the entire point.

At the afternoon meeting that Tilda attended, every person wrote the dangers they could imagine on small slips of paper and dropped them into a wooden box. The slips included the possibility of fewer printed pages in the world, the retirement of key staff, the loss of a major customer and a flood of cheaper imports. One of them, written in Joss's careful hand, simply said that they might get too pleased with themselves.

The group sorted the slips into piles and chose the two dangers that seemed both likely and serious, and Tilda and Marta marked them in red. They wrote a short, practical plan for each one and agreed to repeat the exercise in six months, asking what had changed and whether the plans were still the right ones. Nobody was frightened by the exercise, Tilda noticed, because each danger had a plan next to it.

As they walked across the yard at dusk, Mrs Hale told Tilda quietly that she intended to retire in a year, and that she hoped Tilda would spend it learning every part of the mill. Tilda asked, astonished, why she had been chosen, and Mrs Hale answered that she asked honest questions, told hard facts without fear and shared credit more readily than anyone she knew. Tilda stood quite still in the dusk, and for once she could not think of a single reply.

Tilda spent that year working in every part of the mill, and she began on the night shift, where Sam, now a trainer himself, taught her how to run the great machine with a patience that she recognised. She went out with the drivers, sat beside the sales clerks and spent two weeks with the accountants, who showed her how the four gauges were fed. Every night she wrote what she had learned, and by the end the notebook was no longer big enough.

At a small ceremony in the canteen, Mrs Hale retired, thanked everyone by name and placed the ring of old iron keys into Tilda's open hand. Tilda, who had been practising a long speech for weeks, abandoned it at the last moment and said only that she would try to be worthy of the people in the room and those who had come before. It was the shortest speech she had ever made, and everyone agreed that it was also the best she could have given.

As head of the mill, Tilda changed very little at first, which was exactly what she had learned to do. She kept the Monday table, the worry sheet, the card by the great machine and her two Friday lists, and she added only a monthly visit to the night shift, so that she would never lose touch with its workers. The less she changed, the more the mill seemed to trust her, and the more the mill trusted her, the more freely it told her the truth.

Five years after Tilda first walked through the iron gates, Brightwell celebrated its seventy-fifth birthday with a party in the great workshop. A cake stood in the middle of a long table, covered with seventy-five small candles that Sam and Joss had spent an hour arranging, and the mill around it was not dramatically bigger but unmistakably stronger. It was still growing slowly, in exactly the way that old oaks do, adding one thin ring at a time and never once making a fuss about it.

They all came to the party: Mr Pell with a hand-bound book under his arm, Ines Varga with a painting of the mill, and the suppliers, the drivers, the neighbours and many retired workers. The whole circle of people who had trusted Brightwell, year after year, was gathered in a single noisy room, and Tilda realised that this circle was the real answer to her first question. A company lasts, she saw, because enough people, over enough years, truly want it to.

Mr Okafor was asked to make a speech, and he rose to his feet slowly, with his teacup in his hand and the old twinkle in his eye. He thanked everyone else in the room by name, one after another, and finished by saying that he himself had done very little, which, as everybody present knew, was precisely how he had done it so well. The applause went on for a long time, and he looked a little embarrassed by it.

At the end of the evening a new photograph of the whole crew was hung on the long wall in the corridor, next to the one of the night shift and the enormous order. Mr Okafor was in it, but, as usual, he stood at the very back, half hidden behind Joss, and nobody could remember having arranged it that way. Tilda looked along the wall, seventy-five years of ordinary days, and thought that it had never looked more beautiful.

Someone at the party suggested ending the night with fireworks, and for a moment Tilda was tempted, because they would have been splendid over the dark river. Then she caught Mr Okafor's eye and smiled, and instead they lit a single candle and set it in the window beside the old gate, where it burned quietly while the town went to sleep. It was not much to look at, but, as he had once told her, you could read a book by it.

A few weeks later Tilda helped her niece's school garden club to plan its year, sitting at a table covered with seed packets and muddy gloves. She realised that the same lessons worked for any group of people, whether a club, a team or a family, because humility, honest facts, a clear focus and steady habits are not peculiar to paper. The principles were entirely ordinary, but, as she had learned, they were also surprisingly rare.

Tilda closed her notebook at the mill gate in the evening light, having written its last line: be humble, choose good people, face the truth, keep to your focus, practise steady habits and prepare for the future. These are rules of thumb and not laws, and this story is general information, not financial advice, because every company, person and number in it is imagined. The only thing left to do, she decided with a smile, was to walk home through the gate and to begin again on Monday morning.
